Newborn southern right whales typically measure around 500 centimeters [Lb = around 500 centimeters] in length at birth, a dimension that reflects the considerable energetic investment mothers make in a single, large calf. This substantial initial size, combined with a wet weight at birth of approximately 2,000,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 2,000,000 grams], places the neonate among the largest of all mammalian offspring. At the species' typical core body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the gestation period lasts about 365 days [tg = about 365 days], with available records indicating a gestation time of approximately one year. This prolonged uterine development is consistent with the slow life-history pace characteristic of balaenids, allowing for extensive foetal growth and the deposition of substantial blubber reserves essential for thermoregulation in cold southern waters. Field observations confirm that the physical dimensions of the newborn are already formidable, though they represent only a fraction of the massive adult sizes this species will eventually attain.

As the calf matures, it remains nutritionally dependent on its mother for a considerable period. At the mother's maintained body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the weaning process, marking the end of lactation and the transition to independent foraging, typically occurs at approximately 168 days after birth [tx = approximately 168 days after birth] based on studies of mother-calf associations in coastal nursery areas off Argentina and South Africa. This weaning duration is relatively extended compared to many other cetaceans and allows the calf to build substantial body reserves before undertaking the energy-intensive migration to high-latitude feeding grounds. During the suckling stage, the calf grows rapidly, more than doubling its birth length and significantly increasing its mass. The post-weaning juvenile period is a time of continued somatic growth and behavioral development, during which young whales learn critical foraging skills and social behaviors necessary for survival in the open ocean environment.

The transition to reproductive maturity in southern right whales occurs after many years of sustained growth. At a core temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], puberty is attained at approximately 3,650 days since birth [tp = approximately 3,650 days since birth], a delayed maturation typical of large baleen whales that reflects the extensive time required to achieve sufficient body size for successful reproduction. This milestone marks the onset of physiological capability for breeding, though actual first parturition often occurs somewhat later. Females reach their ultimate length at approximately 1,640 centimeters [Li = approximately 1,640 centimeters], while males are somewhat smaller, attaining a maximum body length of roughly 1,500 centimeters [Li = roughly 1,500 centimeters]. These substantial sexual size differences are linked to the different reproductive strategies of each sex, with females requiring larger body volumes to support the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. The long period required for maturation underscores the high parental investment characteristic of this species, as calves must accumulate considerable somatic reserves before reaching reproductive age.

Female southern right whales exhibit a notably slow reproductive rate, consistent with their position as long-lived, capital-breeding cetaceans. Under optimal conditions at their typical core temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is achieved through a single calf produced approximately every three years [Ri = single calf produced approximately every three years], with a litter size of one offspring per reproductive event [N_R_i = one offspring per reproductive event]. This slow pace of reproduction is an adaptation to the enormous energetic cost of producing a precocial calf weighing up to 47,000,000 grams [Wwi = up to 47,000,000 grams] at adult size, representing the ultimate wet weight attainable by females. The long inter-birth interval allows mothers sufficient time to replenish their energy reserves between successive pregnancies, which is critical given the unpredictable nature of prey availability in the Southern Ocean. Such a reproductive strategy makes the species particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic disturbances that can disrupt feeding success.

Southern right whales are among the longest-lived mammals, with a lifespan that can extend to approximately 36,500 days [am = approximately 36,500 days] when considered at their maintained body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This remarkable longevity, equivalent to roughly one hundred years, is consistent with the extremely slow life-history pace observed across all vital rates of this species. Old individuals bearing distinctive patterns of callosities have been re-sighted in field studies spanning more than four decades, confirming survival well into advanced age. The ultimate wet weight of around 47,000,000 grams [Wwi = around 47,000,000 grams] that characterizes full-grown adults is supported by a massive frame that requires decades to attain, and the prolonged lifespan allows many decades of reproductive activity following the late onset of sexual maturity. This life-history strategy, emphasizing high maternal investment in each individual offspring and extended survival, has proven successful over evolutionary time but renders the species highly sensitive to any increase in adult mortality.
